catalog_quote: p.307 (Toaripi, 8.15.1): "Stress: Words of two or three syllables usually take the stress on the penultimate syllable, e.g. haro /háro/ head, sosoru /sosóru/ firefly. There are some exceptions; e.g. faitora /fáitorə/ now. Final diphthongs take the stress as though two syllables, e.g. mapai /mæpái/ hear. ... The same explanation may be advanced to account partly for the final stress of the personal pronouns, ará, I, aré he, she, it, elá we (exclus.) eré they. This final stress distinguishes them from other words having the same form but with the normal penultimate stress (see p.321). ... When the object marker -ro or the genitive marker ve is added, i.e. araro, arave, etc., the stress assumes the normal penultimate position. Where there are four or more syllables, there is a minor stress on the syllable two removed from the main penultimate stress; thus karikara /karikárə/ village. Compounds exhibit this same stress pattern: maeamariti /màeamaríti/ shame. Reduplicated words repeat the stress of the stem, e.g. sirisiri /sírisíri/ dirty ... There is often a reversal of the normal pattern with onomatopoeic words, e.g. kekekeke /kekékeké/ grey Sandpiper" p.350 (Orokolo, 8.17.1): "In stress, juncture, and intonation Orokolo is in agreement with Toaripi." p.294: "The dialects associated with Orokolo - Muru, Aheave, Belepa, Keuru and Opao - all show a close affinity with it" p.296: "Their dialect [Aheave], like Keuru-Belepa and Muro, has close affinity with Orokolo."

new_statements.quote: Stress. In both Orokolo and Toaripi, with words of two or three syllables, the stress is normally on the penultimate syllable. There are some exceptions, the most notable being with the nominative form of the personal pronouns: ara /ará/ 'I', are /aré/ 'he', 'she', 'it'; ere /eré/ 'they'. The stress pattern here has possibly been influenced by the object and genitive markers, the addition of which to a pronoun normalises the stress. ... With words of four or more syllables, the syllable two removed from the main penultimate stress has a minor stress, e.g. karikara /kàrikára/ 'village'. The stress of the stem is repeated in reduplicated words, e.g. hirihiri /hírihíri/ 'dirty'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the word (stated for Orokolo and Toaripi); a final diphthong counts as two syllables (Brown 1973 p.307); nominative personal pronouns are exceptionally final-stressed, reverting to penultimate when suffixed with -ro/-ve.
new_statements.secondary_stress: In words of four or more syllables a minor stress falls two syllables before the penultimate main stress (i.e. alternating leftward: kàrikára); reduplicated words carry the stem stress on each copy.
new_statements.exceptions: Nominative personal pronouns ara, are, ere (final stress); Brown 1973 p.307 adds Toaripi faitora /fáitora/ 'now', havou, pitoo with final stress, and onomatopoeic words reversing the pattern.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule from citation forms; Brown 1973 pp.307-308 adds that noun+modifier and noun+postposition form one phonological word with main stress on the modifier/postposition, and that phrase intonation puts the accent on the last major stressed syllable. IMPORTANT: the statement is made for Orokolo (orok1267) and Toaripi (toar1246), not for Keuru/Ahia by name; Brown treats Keuru-Belepa (Haura Haela) and Aheave as Western Eleman dialects with 'close affinity with Orokolo' (1973 p.296) and includes KR/HH forms in the 1986 dictionary, but never states their stress separately.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted stress statement is for Orokolo (orok1267) and Toaripi (toar1246), the two Eleman languages H.A. Brown described first-hand. Keoru-Ahia (xeu) corresponds to Brown's Western Eleman dialects 'Keuru (Belepa)' = Hae Haela + Haura Haela (Glottolog alt names Keuru, Belepa, Haura Haela) and 'Aheave' (= Ahia, on the Vailala River); Brown 1973 (Table 3, pp.295-296) lists them beside Orokolo and Opao as separate Western Eleman dialects with 'close affinity with Orokolo', and Brown 1986 cites Keuru (KR) and Haura Haela (HH) forms inside the Orokolo dictionary. No source states stress for Keuru or Ahia by name; applying the penultimate rule to keor1235 is an inference from the closest described relative, not a first-hand statement about this glottocode.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing statement (Brown 1986 p.xiv: Orokolo and Toaripi penultimate, pronoun exceptions), which this earlier text of the same author already contains almost word for word; it adds the minor-stress rule for 4+ syllable words, the compound/reduplication behaviour, the onomatopoeia reversal, the juncture shifts, and the explicit classification (pp.295-296) that puts Keuru (Belepa) and Aheave in the Orokolo dialect cluster. The listed part of the work (Appendix H, pp.579-585) is itself silent on stress. Neither this work nor the existing statement describes Keoru-Ahia stress directly; both are about Toaripi/Orokolo.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stated for Toaripi and (by p.350) for Orokolo: main stress on the penultimate syllable of two- and three-syllable words; in words of four or more syllables a minor stress falls two syllables before the main penultimate stress; compounds follow the same pattern and reduplicated words repeat the stem's stress. Keuru and Aheave (= Keoru-Ahia) receive no stress statement of their own; the volume classes them as Western Eleman dialects 'associated with Orokolo' with close affinity to it (pp.295-296), so the penultimate rule reaches Keoru-Ahia only by that grouping. Appendix H's Keuru and Aheave wordlists are unmarked for stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes (Toaripi, p.307): 'Where there are four or more syllables, there is a minor stress on the syllable two removed from the main penultimate stress; thus karikara /karikára/ village. Compounds exhibit this same stress pattern: maeamariti.. shame. Reduplicated words repeat the stress of the stem, e.g. sirisiri, sosorusosoru radiance.' In close juncture (p.308) the adjective carries the major stress and the noun a minor one (tola lareva 'good tree'); a postposition takes the main stress from its noun (uvi voa).
new_statements.exceptions: p.307: 'There are some exceptions; e.g. faitora now'; final diphthongs count as two syllables (mapai 'hear'); the nominative personal pronouns ara 'I', are 'he, she, it', elawe (excl.), ere 'they' have final stress, which 'distinguishes them from other words having the same form but with the normal penultimate stress'; with object marker -ro or genitive ve added (araro, arave) 'the stress assumes the normal penultimate position'; onomatopoeic words often reverse the normal pattern (kekekeke 'grey sandpiper', hohohoho 'sound of water over rocks'); phrase-level juncture shifts the main stress (p.308).
new_statements.identity_note: Brown 1973 (pp.295-296, Table 3) lists Keuru (Belepa) [= Hae Haela + Haura Haela sub-tribes; 'Keuru' is Ray's 1907 and Williams' 1940 name; Belepa the widely used local name] and Aheave [= Aheave Haela, the smallest sub-tribe, on the Vailala River] as Western Eleman dialects with close affinity to Orokolo, and notes that 'by a refinement of analysis Keuru could be regarded as a dialect distinct from Belepa'. ISO 639-3 xeu 'Keoru-Ahia' (change request 2006-104) names Keoru and Ahia as its two major dialects, matching Brown's Keuru/Belepa and Aheave. Appendix H.1 Aheave (p.579) and H.3 Keuru (pp.580-581) are the only Keoru-Ahia data in the volume: Swadesh-100 lists with the apostrophe marking glottal stop and no stress marks. The stress statements at pp.307-308 are explicitly about Toaripi (Eastern Eleman) and at p.350 about Orokolo (Western Eleman); Brown gives no separate phonology for Keuru or Aheave.
